q.q: Which statement best defines data?
o: Facts that have been processed so that they have meaning
Numbers that have been sorted into order by a computer
Values that have been given a context so they can be used
Raw facts and figures that have no meaning or context
q.why: Data is raw facts and figures with no meaning or context. Processed data with context is information.

q.q: Which of these is an example of information rather than data?
o: F, A, A, C, B, B, A, C, D, A, B, C
Mock grades for one Year 12 pupil: F, A, A, C
q.why: Only this option says what the letters describe, so it has context and therefore meaning.

q.q: The digits 180926 could be a date, a product code in a shop or a bank sort code. What does this show?
o: The same data can give different information in different contexts
Data always has exactly one meaning once it has been stored
Information is simply a larger collection of separate data items
Numbers on their own can never be turned into useful information
q.why: The context decides the meaning, so one set of data can become different information.

q.q: A library system takes in book loans, sorts them and prints a list of overdue books. In the input–process–output model, the printed list is…
o: the raw data input to the system
the processing carried out by the system
the hardware part of the system
the information output by the system
q.why: An information system processes data (input) to produce information (output); the overdue list is the output.

q.q: A pupil writes 'Information is data that is useful.' Why would this not earn the mark?
o: It does not say the data has been processed or given context
It should say information is raw facts and figures instead
It should say information is always stored as numbers
It should say information is any data stored in binary
q.why: Mark schemes need the words processed, context or meaning; 'useful' alone is too vague.

q.q: Why do computers store all data in binary?
o: Their electronic switches have only two states, off and on
Binary numbers take up less storage than denary numbers
Binary is the only number system that can represent text
Each switch can store up to 1024 different values at once
q.why: Transistors are either off (0) or on (1), so a two-digit number system is used.

q.q: What is the smallest unit of data?
o: Nibble
Byte
Kilobyte
Bit
q.why: A bit (binary digit) is a single 0 or 1, the smallest unit. A nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8 bits.

q.q: How many bits make one byte?
q.why: A byte is 8 bits. 4 bits is a nibble, and 1024 is the step between bytes and kilobytes.

q.q: How many different bit patterns can one byte hold?
q.why: 2⁸ = 256 patterns, from 00000000 to 11111111. 255 is the largest value, not the number of patterns.

q.q: Which list is in order from largest to smallest?
o: GB, TB, MB, KB
TB, MB, GB, KB
KB, MB, GB, TB
TB, GB, MB, KB
q.why: Each unit is 1024 times the one below it: TB > GB > MB > KB.

q.q: A pupil writes '1 KB = 1024 bits'. What is the mistake?
o: 1 KB is 1000 bits when using the CCEA exam rules
1 KB is 1024 nibbles, because nibbles come after bits
1 KB is 1024 bytes; bits and bytes are linked by 8
1 KB is 8 bits multiplied by 1000 to make 8000 bits
q.why: The 1024 step only starts from bytes upwards; between bits and bytes the link is 8.

q.q: What is 5 MB in KB?
o: 40 KB
q.why: Going to a smaller unit, multiply by 1024: 5 × 1024 = 5120 KB. 5000 uses 1000, which CCEA does not accept.

q.q: How many bits are there in 6 bytes?
o: 0.75 bits
48 bits
24 bits
6144 bits
q.why: Bytes to bits: multiply by 8, so 6 × 8 = 48 bits.

q.q: What is 2048 MB in GB?
o: 16 GB
2 GB
q.why: Going to a bigger unit, divide by 1024: 2048 ÷ 1024 = 2 GB.

q.q: To convert gigabytes into kilobytes you should…
o: multiply by 1024 twice
divide by 1024 twice
multiply by 1024 once
multiply by 1000 twice
q.why: GB → MB → KB is two steps down, so × 1024 × 1024.

q.q: How many 4 MB photos fit on a 2 GB memory card?
q.why: Convert first: 2 × 1024 = 2048 MB; 2048 ÷ 4 = 512. Using 1000 would give 500.

q.q: A 1 GB USB stick stores songs of 3 MB each. How many complete songs fit?
q.why: 1024 ÷ 3 = 341.33, rounded down to 341 because you cannot store part of a song.

q.q: A pupil works out how many 5 MB files fit on an 8 GB card by doing 8 ÷ 5. What is the mistake?
o: The answer should have been rounded up, not down
The 8 should have been divided by 8 to give bytes
The values should have been multiplied, not divided
The two values were not converted into the same unit first
q.why: Both values must be in the same unit: 8 × 1024 = 8192 MB, then 8192 ÷ 5 = 1638 files.

q.q: Which is the best definition of a character set?
o: A list that gives every character its own unique binary code
A list of the fonts that are installed on a computer
The set of keys that appear on a standard keyboard
A list of the words stored in a spell-checker dictionary
q.why: A character set is an agreed list of characters and their binary codes.

q.q: What does ASCII stand for?
o: American Standard Code for International Information
Automatic System Code for Information Interchange
American Software Code for Integrated Information
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
q.why: ASCII is the American Standard Code for Information Interchange.

q.q: The ASCII code for 'a' is 97. What is the code for 'c'?
q.why: Letter codes run in order: a = 97, b = 98, c = 99. 67 is upper-case 'C'.

q.q: How many bytes are needed to store the text 'Go Ulster!' using one byte per character?
o: 10 bytes
8 bytes
9 bytes
80 bytes
q.why: G, o, space, U, l, s, t, e, r and ! make 10 characters; the space and punctuation count. 80 is the number of bits.

q.q: The digit '7' is typed as part of a text message. How is it stored?
o: As the binary number 111
As the denary number 7
As the binary number 0111
As its character code, 00110111
q.why: A digit typed as text is stored by its character code, not as the binary value of the number.

q.q: Why does a message typed on one computer appear exactly the same on another?
o: Both devices use the same character set
Both devices use the same screen resolution
The text is sent as a bitmap image
Both devices have the same amount of RAM
q.why: A shared character set means the same codes are looked up as the same characters.

q.q: Which data type stores whole numbers with no decimal or fractional part?
o: Real
Character
Integer
String
q.why: Integers are whole numbers, positive or negative. Real numbers can have a decimal part.

q.q: Which value is an example of the string data type?
o: Coleraine
M
q.why: A string is a sequence of characters. M is a single character, 12.99 is real and 06/03/2027 is date/time.

q.q: A pupil's height of 1.68 metres should be stored as…
o: integer
real
character
date/time
q.why: It has a decimal part, so it needs the real data type.

q.q: Which statement about real numbers is correct?
o: They must always be written with a decimal part
They can be negative and can have a decimal part
They can only be positive numbers above zero
They cannot include whole numbers such as 7
q.why: Real numbers include negatives, decimals and whole numbers too, so 7 is real as well as integer.

q.q: Which date format shows 'Saturday, 6 March 2027'?
o: Medium date
Short date
Long date
Long time
q.why: Long date writes the day and month in full. Medium date is 06-Mar-2027 and short date is 06/03/2027.

q.q: What is the difference between a character and a string?
o: A character holds letters only; a string holds digits only
A character can be any length; a string is exactly one symbol
A character is exactly one symbol; a string is a sequence of characters
A character can be used in calculations; a string never can
q.why: A character is one letter, digit or symbol; a string is a sequence of characters of any length.

q.q: Why must data be given a data type before it is processed?
o: So the data is shown in a suitable font and colour when it appears on screen
So the computer knows which operations, such as calculating or sorting, are possible
So the computer can decide which users are allowed to open and read the data
So the data is automatically compressed before it is saved to the storage drive
q.why: The type decides whether data can be calculated, sorted, searched or joined.

q.q: Exam marks such as 100 and 20 are stored as text and then sorted. What problem is likely?
o: Both marks are deleted because text values cannot be sorted
100 is placed before 20 because text sorts character by character
The two marks are added together to make 120 before sorting
20 is rounded down to 2 because text cannot hold two digits
q.why: Text sorts one character at a time, so '1' comes before '2' and 100 appears before 20.

q.q: How does defining a field as integer help keep the data accurate?
o: A type check can make sure each number typed is the true value
It stops the field from ever being left blank by the user
A type check can reject entries such as 'twelve' or '12.5'
It corrects any number that has been typed in the wrong order
q.why: A type check rejects data of the wrong kind, but it cannot prove a number is the right one.

q.q: Which is a storage reason for defining data types in advance?
o: Every file is made exactly one kilobyte in size so it is easy to manage
The type decides which backup drive the data will be copied on to
Text can then be stored as pixels, which take up less space than codes
The right amount of space is reserved and the value is held in the right form
q.why: Each type takes a known amount of space, so the computer can reserve the right amount.

q.q: What is the best data type for a phone number such as 028 7034 0000?
o: String
Integer
Real
Date/time
q.why: An integer would lose the leading zero and cannot hold spaces, and phone numbers are never used in calculations.

q.q: What is the best data type for a pupil's date of birth?
o: Date/time
Integer
String
Real
q.why: Date/time lets the date be sorted and used in calculations such as working out age.

q.q: Why is it better to store a member's date of birth than their age?
o: A date of birth takes up less storage space than an age
Age can be worked out from it and it stays correct as time passes
Ages cannot be stored using the integer data type
A date of birth can be stored as a single character
q.why: An age goes out of date every year, but a date of birth does not and can be used to calculate age.

q.q: A form asks 'Has the fee been paid? (Y/N)'. Which data type from the Unit 1 list is best?
o: String
Integer
Real
Character
q.why: The answer is always exactly one symbol, Y or N, so character fits. (A database would also offer a Boolean Yes/No field.)

q.q: What is the best data type for the price of a cinema ticket, £7.85?
o: Integer
Real
String
Character
q.why: A price needs a decimal part, so it is real (a database may call it currency).

q.q: Which justification for choosing integer for 'number of pupils on a trip' would earn the mark?
o: It is a number, so it has to be a numeric type
It is short, so it will take up very little space
It is a whole number used to count the pupils going
It is data that will be saved in the trip file
q.why: A good justification refers to a feature of the data itself: a whole-number count.

q.q: What is a pixel?
o: A dot of ink placed on paper by an inkjet printer when printing
A shape stored with its position, size and fill colour in a file
The smallest element of a digital image that can be displayed or edited
The number of bits used to store the colour of an image
q.why: Pixel is short for picture element: the smallest part of a digital image.

q.q: What is colour depth?
o: The number of pixels across and down an image
The number of different colours used in the image so far
The number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel
The number of pixels in each inch of a screen
q.why: Colour depth is bits per pixel; n bits give 2ⁿ possible colours.

q.q: How many colours can be shown with a colour depth of 8 bits?
q.why: 2⁸ = 256 colours, which is the GIF limit.

q.q: An image needs 100 different colours. What is the smallest colour depth that works?
o: 6 bits
7 bits
8 bits
100 bits
q.why: 6 bits give only 64 colours; 7 bits give 128, which is enough.

q.q: Why does a bitmap file store the image's width as metadata?
o: So the computer knows where each row of pixels ends
So the image can be compressed without losing data
So every pixel can be given a different colour
So the image can be enlarged without pixelation
q.why: Without the width, the computer could not rebuild the grid of pixels row by row.

q.q: What does a resolution of 1920 × 1080 tell you?
o: The image is 1920 pixels down and 1080 pixels across
The image is 1920 pixels across and 1080 pixels down
The image uses 1920 colours stored in 1080 bits
The image is 1920 KB and takes 1080 ms to load
q.why: Resolution is written width × height, so the first number is across and the second is down.

q.q: Which unit gives screen resolution as a density?
o: dpi
ppi
Hz
kbps
q.why: Pixels per inch is used for screens; dots per inch is used for printing.

q.q: An image's resolution changes from 800 × 600 to 1600 × 1200 with the same colour depth. What happens to the file size?
o: It becomes about twice as big
It becomes about 8 times as big
It stays about the same
It becomes about 4 times as big
q.why: Width and height both double, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 times as many pixels to store.

q.q: Which two factors decide the size of an uncompressed bitmap?
o: Resolution and screen size
Colour depth and file format
Resolution and colour depth
Number of objects and their properties
q.why: Every pixel must be stored using the colour depth number of bits. Objects and properties describe vectors.

q.q: A pupil says 'a higher resolution makes the pixels bigger'. What is the correct statement?
o: A higher resolution means there are more pixels in the image
A higher resolution means each pixel uses more bits of colour
A higher resolution means each pixel takes less storage
A higher resolution means fewer pixels but much sharper ones
q.why: Resolution is the number of pixels, so higher resolution means more pixels and more detail. Bits per pixel is colour depth.

q.q: What does a bitmap graphic file store?
o: The colour code of every pixel plus metadata
A list of objects and the properties of each
Only the width, height and colour depth
Instructions for redrawing each shape
q.why: A bitmap holds every pixel's colour code row by row, plus metadata such as width, height and colour depth.

q.q: What happens when a vector graphic is resized?
o: Each pixel is simply drawn larger than it was before
Extra pixels are copied in to fill the gaps between them
The file is decompressed, resized and then saved again
Its objects are recalculated mathematically and redrawn
q.why: A vector stores objects as mathematical descriptions, so it is redrawn at the new size and stays sharp.

q.q: A logo file contains 'circle: centre=(150, 60), radius=40, fill=gold'. What type of graphic is this?
o: A bitmap graphic storing the colour of each pixel
A bitmap graphic storing the image's metadata
A vector graphic storing a grid of coloured pixels
A vector graphic storing an object and its properties
q.why: Position, size and fill colour are properties of an object, which is how vectors are stored.

q.q: Which type of graphic stays sharp when it is enlarged to any size?
o: Bitmap graphic
JPEG photograph
Vector graphic
PNG screenshot
q.why: Vectors are recalculated when resized. JPEG and PNG are bitmap formats, so they pixelate.

q.q: Why are vector graphics not suitable for photographs?
o: Vector graphics can only display images in black and white
Describing every subtle change of colour as shapes would be impractical
Vector files are always far larger than bitmap files
Vector graphics cannot be displayed on a computer screen
q.why: Photos contain endless tiny colour changes that cannot sensibly be stored as objects.

q.q: How does editing a bitmap differ from editing a vector?
o: A bitmap is changed object by object; a vector is changed pixel by pixel
A bitmap is changed pixel by pixel; a vector is changed object by object
Both are changed only by editing the metadata stored in the file
A bitmap cannot be edited at all once it has been saved to disk
q.why: Bitmaps are made of pixels and vectors of objects, so that is what you edit in each.

q.q: Why does a small, low-resolution photo look poor when printed on a large poster?
o: The printer removes some pixels to save ink when printing large posters
The photo is changed into a vector, which loses most of its colours
Each pixel is drawn larger, so blocks show and no new detail is added
Enlarging the photo lowers its colour depth to 1 bit per pixel
q.why: This is pixelation: the same pixels are simply drawn bigger, so edges look jagged.

q.q: A GAA club wants one crest for its website, its jerseys and a large pitch-side banner. Which is best?
o: A bitmap, because it can be scaled without losing quality
A vector, because it can be scaled without losing quality
A bitmap, because bitmaps are best for logos and diagrams
A vector, because it stores the colour of every pixel
q.why: Vectors suit logos and stay sharp at any size; bitmaps pixelate when enlarged.

q.q: What is the formula for the size of a bitmap image in bits?
o: width × height × number of colours
width × height × colour depth
width × height ÷ colour depth
(width + height) × colour depth
q.why: Each of the width × height pixels needs colour-depth bits. Using the number of colours is a common error.

q.q: A 16 × 16 icon uses 4-bit colour. What is its size in bytes?
o: 1024 bytes
64 bytes
4096 bytes
128 bytes
q.why: 16 × 16 × 4 = 1024 bits, ÷ 8 = 128 bytes. 1024 is the size in bits, not bytes.

q.q: An 800 × 600 image uses 8-bit colour. What is its size in KB?
o: 480 KB
q.why: 800 × 600 × 8 = 3 840 000 bits ÷ 8 = 480 000 bytes ÷ 1024 = 468.75 KB. 480 KB comes from wrongly dividing by 1000.

q.q: A 100 × 100 image is 30 000 bytes. What is its colour depth?
o: 24 bits
3 bits
8 bits
30 bits
q.why: 30 000 bytes × 8 = 240 000 bits; 240 000 ÷ 10 000 pixels = 24 bits per pixel. 3 comes from forgetting to multiply by 8.

q.q: A pupil calculates the size of a 50 × 50 image with 256 colours as 50 × 50 × 256. What is the error?
o: They should have added 50 and 50 instead of multiplying them
They used the number of colours instead of the bits per pixel (8)
They should have divided 256 by 1024 before multiplying
They forgot to multiply the answer by 1024 to get bits
q.why: 256 colours need 8 bits per pixel, so the calculation should be 50 × 50 × 8 bits.

q.q: A 1920 × 1080 image uses 24-bit colour. What is its size in bytes?
o: 2 073 600 bytes
6 220 800 bytes
6075 bytes

q.q: Why must sound be converted before a computer can store it?
o: Sound is digital but computers only process analogue signals
Sound files are too large to store unless they are converted
Sound is analogue but computers only process digital (binary) data
Microphones produce binary that must be changed into sound
q.why: Sound is a continuously varying analogue wave; a computer needs binary.

q.q: What does an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) do?
o: Turns stored binary numbers back into a smooth electrical signal
Picks up vibrations in the air and turns them into an electrical signal
Measures the signal at regular intervals and stores each sample in binary
Compresses the recording so that it takes up less storage space
q.why: The ADC samples the analogue signal and stores each sample as a binary number. The microphone picks up the sound; a DAC plays it back.

q.q: Which describes sampling?
o: Measuring the height of the wave once at the start of the recording
Recording the wave continuously with no gaps between readings
Removing sounds that people are unlikely to be able to hear
Measuring the height of the sound wave at regular time intervals
q.why: Sampling measures the amplitude at regular intervals; each measurement is a sample.

q.q: Why is a digital sound recording always an approximation of the original?
o: The microphone removes some sounds before they reach the computer
Binary can only store whole numbers that are between 0 and 255
Every recording is compressed using lossy compression when saved
The wave is measured only at set moments and each reading is rounded
q.why: Detail between samples is missed and each sample is rounded to the nearest level.

q.q: What is sample rate?
o: The number of samples taken every second
The number of bits used to store each sample
The number of bits processed every second
The number of levels each sample can take
q.why: Sample rate is samples per second, measured in hertz. Bits per sample is bit depth; bits per second is bit rate.

q.q: What sample rate is used for CD-quality audio?
o: 16 Hz
q.why: CDs use 44 100 Hz (44.1 kHz). 16 is the CD bit depth and 65 536 is the number of 16-bit levels.

q.q: What is bit depth?
o: The number of samples taken each second
The number of bits processed per second of sound
The number of bits used to store each sample
The number of channels used in the recording
q.why: Bit depth is bits per sample; n bits give 2ⁿ levels.

q.q: What happens if the sample rate of a recording is too low?
o: Each sample is rounded roughly, adding hiss
The file becomes larger than it needs to be
The recording changes from stereo to mono
Changes in the wave between samples are missed
q.why: Too few samples cannot follow the wave's shape. Rough rounding and hiss come from too low a bit depth.

q.q: A recording is changed from mono to stereo, with everything else the same. What is the effect?
o: The amount of data halves
The bit depth doubles
The amount of data doubles
The amount of data stays the same
q.why: Stereo has two channels (left and right), so twice as much data is stored as mono.

q.q: Which is the formula for bit rate?
o: sample rate × bit depth × length in seconds
sample rate × bit depth × number of channels
sample rate ÷ bit depth × number of channels
bit depth × number of channels × 8
q.why: Bit rate is bits per second: sample rate × bit depth × channels. Multiplying by length gives the file size.

q.q: What is the bit rate of CD audio at 44 100 Hz, 16-bit, stereo?
q.why: 44 100 × 16 × 2 = 1 411 200 bits per second. 705 600 forgets the second channel.

q.q: An 8000 Hz, 8-bit, mono recording lasts 60 seconds. What is its size in bytes?
o: 3 840 000 bytes
480 000 bytes
64 000 bytes
468.75 bytes

q.q: A 2-minute stereo clip is recorded at 22 050 Hz with 16-bit samples. What is its size in bytes?
o: 5 292 000 bytes
176 400 bytes
q.why: 22 050 × 16 × 2 × 120 = 84 672 000 bits ÷ 8 = 10 584 000 bytes. 5 292 000 forgets stereo; 176 400 uses 2 instead of 120 seconds.

q.q: Which mistake gives a sound file size that is 8 times too big?
o: Forgetting to divide by 8 to turn bits into bytes
Forgetting to multiply by 2 for a stereo recording
Forgetting to change the minutes into seconds
Using 1000 instead of 1024 when finding kilobytes
q.why: The formula gives bits; not dividing by 8 leaves the answer 8 times too large.

q.q: Why does a real MP3 file take far less space than the formula gives for the recording?
o: MP3 always records at a much lower sample rate
MP3 is a compressed format, so it stores much less data
MP3 files only ever store one channel of sound
MP3 stores instrument instructions instead of sound
q.why: The formula gives the uncompressed size; MP3 uses lossy compression. Storing instructions describes MIDI.

q.q: What is streaming?
o: Downloading the whole video file first so that it can be played back afterwards
Saving a video permanently on the device so it can be watched without a connection
Compressing a video so that it is small enough to send as an email attachment
Playing video or audio as it arrives in small pieces, without waiting for the whole file
q.why: Streaming starts playback as soon as the first pieces arrive; the file is not normally kept.

q.q: While a video streams, what does the buffer hold?
o: The next part of the video, stored temporarily in memory
The whole video, stored permanently on the device
The parts already watched, kept so they can be replayed
A compressed copy of the full video file for later
q.why: The buffer is temporary memory that holds a small part of the video ahead of where you are watching.

q.q: When does a streamed video pause and show a loading icon?
o: When the buffer has become completely full
Whenever the connection slows down slightly
When the buffer has emptied completely
When the video reaches the start of a new scene
q.why: Playback only stops when there is no data left in the buffer; brief slowdowns are covered by buffered data.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of streaming compared with downloading?
o: It needs an internet connection all the time you are watching
You must wait for the whole file before playback can start
It uses far more storage space on the device than downloading
It cannot be used for live events such as sports matches
q.why: Streaming needs a continuous connection; a downloaded file works offline once saved.

q.q: Which is the best definition of data portability?
o: Carrying data from place to place on a USB stick or a mobile phone
Moving data between computers or applications without having to re-enter it
Compressing data so that it is small enough to be sent by email
Storing data in the cloud so that it can be reached from anywhere
q.why: Portability means transferring data without retyping it. Carrying a USB stick is not data portability.

q.q: How do standard file formats support data portability?
o: Many different programs on different systems can open them
They make files small enough to fit on portable devices
They lock each file so only one program can open it
They change all data into plain text before saving it
q.why: A standard format is understood by many programs on Windows, macOS, Android and iOS.

q.q: Which list contains only audio formats?
o: mp3, mp4, wav, avi
wav, wma, mpeg, midi
mp3, wav, wma, midi
midi, mp3, tiff, wma
q.why: mp4, avi and mpeg are video formats and tiff is an image format.

q.q: A school sends results to an exam board electronically in a standard format instead of retyping them. Which benefit of data portability does this show?
o: It means the results no longer need to be backed up anywhere
It makes the results file smaller so it uploads more quickly
It guarantees that every result in the file is correct
It saves time and avoids errors because data is not re-entered
q.why: Portability avoids retyping, which saves time and avoids transcription errors.

q.q: Which image format uses lossless compression and supports transparency?
o: JPEG
TIFF
PNG
PICT
q.why: PNG keeps quality with lossless compression and supports transparency, so it suits logos.

q.q: Which format stores notes, instrument and timing instructions rather than recorded sound?
o: MIDI
WAV
MP3
WMA
q.why: MIDI holds instructions for an instrument, giving tiny files; WAV, MP3 and WMA store sound.

q.q: A teacher wants a worksheet to keep exactly the same fonts, images and layout when parents open it. Which format?
o: PDF
RTF
TXT
CSV
q.why: PDF fixes fonts, images and layout. RTF keeps only basic formatting and TXT has none.

q.q: Which is the best justification for using JPEG for photos on a club website?
o: It is a vector format, so the photos stay sharp at any size
Its compression gives small files that load quickly on a web page
It stores the photos without losing any of the original data
It can store a series of images to make a simple animation
q.why: JPEG's lossy compression makes small files with millions of colours. It is lossy, not lossless, and animation is GIF.

q.q: A band is recording and editing songs in a studio. Which format is best for the raw recordings?
o: MP3, because it is uncompressed and high quality
MIDI, because it records the actual sound waves
WMA, because it is the standard for editing sound
WAV, because it is uncompressed and high quality
q.why: WAV is uncompressed, so no quality is lost while editing. MP3 is lossy and MIDI stores instructions, not sound.

q.q: Which is a Microsoft video format that keeps audio and video in sync but is often large?
o: AVI
MPEG
MP4
WMA
q.why: AVI is Microsoft's video format. WMA is Microsoft's audio format; MPEG and MP4 are compressed video formats.

q.q: Which is NOT a benefit of compressing files?
o: It improves the quality of photos and sound
More files fit on a memory card or phone
Files upload and download more quickly
Streaming uses less of a mobile data allowance
q.why: Compression reduces size; it never adds quality, and lossy compression lowers it.

q.q: Which answer best explains how compression helps when uploading a video to a website?
o: Compression increases the upload speed of the internet connection itself
The video is changed to a higher resolution before it is uploaded
Less data needs to be sent, so the upload is faster and uses less bandwidth
The video is held in a buffer so the upload never pauses part-way
q.why: A smaller file means less data to transfer, so transfer time falls and bandwidth is saved.

q.q: Which is an example of lossy compression?
o: ZIP
PNG
GIF
MP3
q.why: MP3 removes sounds people are unlikely to notice. ZIP, PNG and GIF are lossless.

q.q: Which statement describes lossless compression?
o: Some data is removed permanently to make the file much smaller
No data is lost, so the original can be restored exactly
Data is removed but can be rebuilt later from the metadata
The file is made smaller by lowering its resolution
q.why: Lossless compression stores the same data more efficiently, so decompression gives an exact copy.

q.q: How might lossless compression store a row of twenty white pixels?
o: As one white pixel, removing the other nineteen for good
As '20 white pixels' instead of twenty identical codes
As twenty pixels that each use a lower colour depth
As a single vector shape with a white fill colour
q.why: It finds a more efficient way to store exactly the same information, so nothing is lost.

q.q: A photographer is uploading a large photo to a news website, where a small loss of quality is acceptable. Which compression suits best?
o: Lossy, because it gives a much larger reduction in file size
Lossless, because it gives a much larger reduction in file size
Lossy, because the original photo can be restored exactly
Lossless, because some data is permanently removed
q.why: Lossy compression shrinks files much more and suits photos where a small loss is not noticed.

q.q: Why must a program file be compressed losslessly?
o: Program files cannot be made any smaller by lossy methods
Lossy compression only works on plain text files
Losing even one bit could stop the program working
Lossless compression gives smaller files than lossy
q.why: Every bit of a program matters, so it must be restored exactly. Lossless gives less reduction than lossy, not more.
